sections.text: Adapters build a pipeline, and a consumer runs it. A consuming method keeps calling next until the iterator ends and gives back a result. Which one you choose decides what you get: a collection, a number, an Option or a bool.

collect gathers items into a collection. It can build many kinds: a Vec, a String, a HashMap. Rust needs to know which, so you say it with a type annotation on the variable, or with ::<Type> after collect (that odd-looking ::<> is called the turbofish). A _ lets Rust fill in the part it can already work out.

Other consumers turn the whole sequence into one value. sum adds the items up, and count says how many there are. fold is the general one: you give it a starting value and a closure that takes the running total (acc) and the next item, and returns the new total.
min and max return an Option, because an empty iterator has no smallest item. find returns the first item that matches, also as an Option.
any and all answer yes or no: does at least one item match, or do all of them?

nums.iter() hands out references (&i32), and some methods pass your closure another reference on top of that. find does, so its closure sees a &&i32 and **n unwraps both layers. any and all pass the item as it is, so n is a &i32: n % 2 works on a reference, but a comparison like *n > 0 needs the star. When the types look confusing, the compiler error tells you exactly which one it expected.

sum needs to know what type to add up. That is why total has a type annotation: i32. You can also write nums.iter().sum::<i32>(). max and min give back Option<&i32>, a reference into the Vec. References print like the value they point to, so {:?} shows Some(42), as in the Output comment.
A pipeline usually ends with one consumer. Count the words in a sentence that are longer than three letters:

split_whitespace gives an iterator over the words, so every adapter and consumer in this lesson works on it. max_by_key picks the item with the biggest key from the closure. If several are tied, it returns the last one.
Think of collect as "empty the conveyor belt into a box", and sum, count and max as "just give me one number from the belt". Both consume the iterator, so it can't be used again afterwards.

Equivalents: Python sum(), len(list(...)), max(), any(), all(), functools.reduce (fold); Java collect(Collectors.toList()), reduce, anyMatch, allMatch; JS reduce, some, every, find. A nice Rust trick: collect can gather an iterator of Results into one Result<Vec<_>, _>, stopping at the first Err, for example let nums: Result<Vec<i32>, _> = ["1", "2"].iter().map(|s| s.parse::<i32>()).collect();

exercise.prompt: The starter adds up word lengths with a for loop and prints 9. Replace the loop with an iterator pipeline that maps each word to its length and sums them, keeping the printed total. Then, on a new line, print how many of the words are longer than 2 bytes, counted with filter and count. It should print two lines: 9 and 2. Hint: the total needs a type, so write let total: usize = ... and end the pipeline with .sum().

quiz.question: Which of these is a consuming method, not an adapter?
options: sum, because it runs the whole iterator and returns one value
map, because it applies the closure to every item in the pipeline
filter, because it decides which items stay in the pipeline

quiz.question: Why does max() return an Option?
options: max can fail to compare two numbers, for example when one is negative
max needs a closure, and the closure might not give a result
An empty iterator has no largest item, so there may be nothing to return

quiz.question: How does collect() know whether to build a Vec, a String or a HashMap?
options: It always builds a Vec, and you convert it afterwards
From the type annotation or the turbofish, such as Vec<i32> or ::<String>
From the type of the first item the iterator produces
